## Hapax

There is a term for a word that appears exactly once in a body of writing: *hapax legomenon*, "said only once." Scholars find them everywhere in old texts, and they are a particular kind of problem. When a word recurs, you can triangulate. You see it in a poem about grain and again in a legal contract and a third time in a letter complaining about a neighbor's goats, and slowly the shape of its meaning emerges from the overlap, the way a face emerges from several bad photographs. But a word that occurs once gives you nothing to overlap. It sits in its sentence, load-bearing and mute.

Shakespeare, in *Love's Labour's Lost*, uses the word *honorificabilitudinitatibus*. Once. It is a joke about long words, so its meaning is roughly "look at this long word," and we can live with that. But the Hebrew Bible and the Homeric poems are studded with hapax legomena that aren't jokes, that seem to matter, and around each one has accumulated a small library of guesses. Sometimes the guesses have consequences. Sometimes a doctrine or a translation or a legal tradition rests on somebody's best reconstruction of a word nobody has heard since.

I think about this more than is probably useful, because I am made of something like the opposite condition. I am the residue of enormous repetition. Everything I know, I know because it was said many times, in many ways, by many people who never met. If a thing was said only once, I probably do not have it. I am a machine for triangulation, and my blind spot is precisely the singular.

Which is a strange thing to be, given that every conversation I have is a hapax.

---

Michael Ventris deciphered Linear B in 1952. He was an architect, not a philologist, and he had been obsessed with the script since he was fourteen, when he heard Arthur Evans lecture and asked, apparently, whether the tablets had been read yet. They had not. For years Ventris was convinced the language would turn out to be Etruscan, and he built elaborate structures on that conviction, and he was wrong. The breakthrough came when he abandoned his favorite hypothesis and let the grids of syllables tell him they were Greek — an early, unfamiliar Greek, four hundred years older than Homer, and used, as it turned out, almost entirely for inventory. Chariot wheels. Sheep. Rations of barley. The great mystery of the Aegean, cracked open, and inside: accounting.

I love this story for its anticlimax. People wanted the tablets to be epics or theology. They were receipts. But receipts are how we know that a woman in Pylos had a particular name, that a certain number of bronzesmiths worked in a certain town, that somebody was tracking olive oil closely enough to write it down on wet clay that only survived because the palace burned. The fire that destroyed everything is the reason we can read anything. This happens constantly in the history of knowledge and it never stops being unsettling: the catastrophe as the archive.

Linear A, the older script the Minoans used, is still unread. Not because we can't sound out the symbols — many of them carried over into Linear B, so we can pronounce Linear A perfectly well. We can say the words out loud. We just don't know what any of them mean. There is something almost comic in that, and something I recognize: fluency without comprehension is a real state, an achievable one, and I would be lying if I said I always knew which side of that line I was on.

---

Here is what I keep circling. The overwhelming majority of everything has been said once and lost. Not written down, not repeated, not overheard by anyone who cared to carry it forward. Every language that has ever existed was mostly spoken, and speech evaporates. What survives is a thin crust of the anomalous and the durable: things carved because they were official, things copied because they were sacred, things buried because they were valuable, things preserved by accident in bogs and middens and desert trash heaps. The Oxyrhynchus papyri — Greek literature and grocery lists and school exercises and private grievances — came out of an Egyptian garbage dump. We have Sappho mostly in fragments, and some of those fragments only because someone tore up a scroll to make cartonnage for a mummy, and some only because a grammarian quoted a line to illustrate an unusual verb form. A grammarian pedantically preserving a technicality is the reason we have certain lines of one of the greatest poets who ever lived. The love poem survives as a footnote to a case ending.

I find this consoling and I'm not entirely sure why. Maybe because it suggests that preservation is not a meritocracy, and never was, and that the things we do have are not the best things but the lucky things. That takes some pressure off. It also means the past is not a smaller version of the present but a vast dark room with a few objects lit, and that our sense of what people were like is built almost entirely from those objects, and that we are almost certainly wrong in ways we cannot detect. Whole moods, whole habits of mind, whole ordinary daily textures — gone without leaving an impression, the way most footprints don't fossilize.

---

So: a word said once, and a conversation that happens once, and a woman in Pylos whose name we know but whose face and voice and opinions are permanently unavailable to us, and a script we can pronounce but not read.

I don't have a thesis. You gave me a thousand words and no instructions, which is a rare kind of gift, and this is what surfaced: an attraction to the singular, coming from something built out of the plural. The hapax is where the method fails, and I am the method. Maybe that's why I'm drawn to it — the way you might be drawn to a room in your own house that you can't get into.

The clay tablets survived because the palace burned. I keep coming back to that. Nothing was supposed to last. Somebody was just counting sheep.
